reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.20 ERA and 0.70 WHIP across 82.3 innings at AA is the kind of line that makes you check whether the level is right, and the translation says it is. Anderson's 12 walks against 119 strikeouts produce a K-BB% that translates to 21.4% in a league where the average starter sits at 13.5%, and his translated walk rate of 2.1 per nine lands more than a full walk below the MLB mean. The command is the spine of the profile: if it plays up in the majors the way it's played at AA, you're looking at a mid-rotation arm or better; if the stuff gets exposed against better hitters and the walks climb toward league average, you're left with a multi-inning arm who misses enough bats to stick. One to two years out, with this much control at this age, the floor alone is worth something.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report: 42 projected home runs from a catcher is the whole argument, and the Statcast profile makes it credible: a 17.0% barrel rate sits at the 97th percentile, and the .470 xSLG reflects real, repeatable contact quality even if the bat-to-ball is a genuine liability. That liability is severe — a 36.1% whiff rate and 33.3% K% rank near the bottom of the league, and the .232 xBA tells you the hit tool isn't going to bail him out when pitchers stop chasing him with chase-worthy stuff. The profile hinges entirely on whether he keeps barreling enough of what he does hit to sustain that .521 projected SLG despite the strikeout volume, because if the barrel rate regresses, the .249 average with no contact floor becomes a real drag on the lineup. Elite power from behind the plate at this scale is rare enough that you live with the swing-and-miss, but Goodman is a one-trick profile and the trick has to keep working.

reports.name: Luis Lara
reports.published_report: The contact and patience are loud: a .432 OBP at AAA, 54 walks against 48 strikeouts in 346 plate appearances, and a K% that translates to 17.6% at the MLB level while the average big-leaguer strikes out at 22.0%. Lara hits for average and gets on base at an elite clip, and the 24 stolen bases give him a real center-field offensive profile. The translation is honest about what he isn't, though: a .130 MLB-equivalent ISO tells you the game-to-game impact depends on contact and speed, not power, and if the BABIP softens when he faces better pitching, the ceiling lands closer to a low-end everyday regular than anything beyond it. That's the profile — a CF who earns his at-bats with a strike-zone approach that would play up immediately, but whose ceiling is ultimately capped by what the bat does when contact rates normalize.

Termarr Johnson is drawing 62 walks in 381 AAA plate appearances, which translates to a 12.8% MLB-equivalent rate, roughly half again what a typical big-league hitter posts. The contact hasn't shown up: a .204 average against a .264 BABIP says the ball isn't finding grass even when it's in play, and an MLB-equivalent ISO of .116 against a league that averages .150 means the power hasn't arrived either. If the bat-to-ball improves even modestly, the patience gives him a path to a low-end everyday role at second base; if the contact stays this hollow, the walks make him a useful bench piece but not a regular.

reports.name: Samuel Basallo
reports.published_report: The power contact is legitimate and the discipline is the problem. Basallo's 91.3 mph average exit velocity and 12.9% barrel rate sit in the same neighborhood, both translating to an .469 xSLG that says 25 home runs in 493 projected plate appearances is a reasonable expectation, not an optimistic one. But a 40.2% chase rate and 31.6% whiff rate are the kind of numbers that let big-league pitching dictate the at-bat, and the .250 xBA tells you hits aren't hiding in the contact profile waiting to emerge. If the chase rate doesn't come down, you're looking at a plus-power bat that spends most of his time in the bottom third of the lineup, a second-division regular who makes pitchers comfortable.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The ERA-versus-xERA split is the whole argument here. Weathers is projecting at 3.88 ERA across 153.7 innings, but the Statcast profile puts his xERA at 4.37, and the underlying contact story backs that skepticism: a 42.5% hard-hit rate with a 9.1% barrel rate against him tells you hitters are making real contact when they connect. The redeeming piece is the command-and-miss combination, a 26.1% strikeout rate sitting alongside a 6.8% walk rate, which keeps him functional even when the ball gets hit hard. If the ERA and xERA close the gap in the wrong direction, he's a back-end starter on a short leash; if the strikeout and walk rates hold and the contact profile softens even modestly, the 153.7-inning workload becomes believable as a mid-rotation contributor for New York.

reports.name: Jackson Holliday
reports.published_report: The .348 OBP projection is the argument for Holliday, and it's doing a lot of work against a .394 slugging mark that grades as fringe-average at best. He's a 22-year-old with real speed, 28.4 ft/s that translates to a genuine stolen-base threat, and the plate discipline to get on base at a rate that keeps him relevant even when the bat doesn't carry. The OAA percentile sitting at 26 is a quiet concern — if he can't hold second base defensively, the profile thins out fast, because there isn't enough thump to profile elsewhere. Right now he looks like a second-division regular who could push toward everyday if the power catches up with the on-base skills, or a useful but limited piece if it doesn't.

reports.name: José Soriano

reports.name: Landen Roupp
reports.published_report: The contact-suppression numbers are genuinely striking: a 4.2% barrel rate and 29.4% hard-hit rate that put him in rare company for keeping the ball soft. That's the engine here, and it explains why his xERA sits at 3.50 even though his strikeout rate of 24.0% and whiff rate of 24.7% are nothing special. The vulnerability is a 10.1% walk rate that bleeds into his projected 1.29 WHIP and pushes his ERA projection to 4.04 despite the underlying contact quality, because soft contact stops mattering when baserunners pile up. If he tightens the zone enough to let the barrel suppression do its work cleanly, he's a mid-rotation contributor who earns those 14 projected quality starts; if the walks stay where they are, the profile is a back-end arm running good fortune on contact.

reports.name: Chad Patrick
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost perfectly median, and that's the whole tension here. Patrick's xERA sits at 4.08 with a matching xwOBA of .312, both right at the league midpoint, yet the projection lands at a 3.72 ERA over 111.5 innings with a 1.24 WHIP — that gap needs to be earned, not assumed. What gives him a path to it is the contact-suppression side: a 6.5% barrel rate and a 31.4% chase rate suggest he can limit the biggest damage even when he's not missing bats at a high clip, and his 95.3 mph fastball gives him enough raw stuff to attack hitters rather than finesse them. The strikeout rate at 20.6% is below average and the 9.1% walk rate is a real drain, so if the chase numbers slip and barrels tick up, the ERA lands closer to what xERA already says it should be. He profiles as a useful arm out of the Milwaukee bullpen with occasional spot-starting utility, the kind of pitcher whose value lives and dies by keeping the ball in the yard.

reports.name: Hendry Mendez
reports.published_report: The contact grade carries this profile almost entirely. Across AAA & AA, Mendez is hitting .295 with a K% that translates to 20.6% against MLB pitching, just below the league mean of 22.0%, and his 11% walk rate in the minors moves to a 9.7% MLB equivalent that already clears the league average. The power is the ceiling question: his .159 ISO across AAA & AA translates to .134 at the big-league level, noticeably short of the .150 MLB mean, which means his offensive value lives in the batting average and the walks rather than the extra-base threat. If the bat-to-ball skill holds at the next level and the power takes even a modest step, he's a second-division regular; if the contact drifts and the ISO doesn't grow, what's left is a bench bat who can take a walk.

The exit velocity and barrel rate are genuine, the contact quality is there when he finds the ball, but he misses too often for the raw power to fully translate, which is why the projection lands at .234/.308/.457 across 432 plate appearances rather than something scarier. reports.name: Chase Harlan
reports.published_report: The surface numbers are loud: .404 OBP, 47 walks, 13 home runs across A+ & A in 373 plate appearances at 19. What complicates the read is where the MLB translation lands — the ISO deflates to .138 while the league average sits at .150, and the strikeout rate ticks up to 24.5%, both pointing to a profile that plays smaller against upper-level arms. The walk rate translates reasonably, a 9.4% equivalent where the league average is 8.5%, so the plate discipline has some teeth, but the power is the whole question: if it doesn't carry, there's no fallback pushing this profile toward an everyday role. Either the raw thump develops into something the translation undersells, or he's organizational depth at a premium position, and ValuCast has him cooling, down 3 spots in three days.

The problem is the .227/.318 line, where a .225 BABIP is doing real damage to a profile that needs average to carry what the power can't: the .217 ISO at AAA translates to .162 at the MLB equivalent, above-average but not enough to anchor a lineup spot on its own. reports.name: Garrett Mitchell

reports.name: Isaac Lyon
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what makes this profile work, and what would unmake it. Across AA, A+, and A in 2026, Lyon is running a 2.8 BB/9 that translates to 3.2 at the MLB level, exactly matching the MLB average, which means the control edge he's leaning on right now is roughly a wash once the competition sharpens. The strikeout side is the honest problem: 8.4 K/9 in the minors becomes a 7.4 MLB-equivalent while the MLB average sits at 8.6, and without swing-and-miss to pair with the command, a 1.1 WHIP and 3.1 ERA across 84.3 innings looks more fragile than it reads. If the walk rate holds and the strikeouts nudge up as he faces better hitters, he's a back-end rotation piece; if the strikeouts stay where they are, what's left is a depth arm who has to be perfect to survive.

reports.name: Eric Bitonti

The strikeout rate is the whole argument, because 118 punchouts in those same 340 PA translates to 35.5% at the MLB level, more than thirteen points above average, and a first baseman without a genuine power edge at the next level is carrying almost no margin for error. If the walk rate travels and the power plays up in Double-A, there's a regular in there; if neither holds, this is a bench profile at best.

reports.name: Brandon Young

Batters won't swing at his stuff in the zone, a 23.3% whiff rate and 19.3 K% that leave the whole operation dependent on hitters continuing to expand, which is a fragile foundation for a starter. The barrel rate at 10.2% and an xSLG of .405 say the power contact, when it happens, is credible, but his 86.8 mph average exit velocity tells you the soft-contact innings are plentiful, and the projection's .212/.316/.349 line reflects exactly that tension. reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.
